## Solution

**Claim.** The Lindenbaum–Tarski σ-algebra $A$ of $L_{\omega_1}$ is **atomless**; in particular, it contains no atoms.

### Key observation: every formula has countable support

Define the *support* $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$ of a formula $\varphi$ as the set of propositional variables occurring in it. We prove by induction on formula complexity that $|\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)|\le\aleph_0$ for every formula of $L_{\omega_1}$.

- **Atomic** $p_\alpha$: $\operatorname{supp}(p_\alpha)=\{p_\alpha\}$, countable. ✓
- **Negation** $\neg\varphi$: $\operatorname{supp}(\neg\varphi)=\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$, countable by induction. ✓
- **Countable disjunction/conjunction** $\bigvee_{i<\lambda}\varphi_i$ / $\bigwedge_{i<\lambda}\varphi_i$ with $\lambda<\omega_1$ (hence $\lambda$ countable): $\operatorname{supp}=\bigcup_{i<\lambda}\operatorname{supp}(\varphi_i)$, a countable union of countable sets, hence countable. ✓

Since the language has $\omega_1$ propositional variables, for **every** formula $\varphi$ there exists a variable $p\notin\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$.

### The algebra is atomless

Let $[\varphi]\in A$ be any nonzero element, i.e., $\varphi$ is satisfiable. Let $S=\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$ (countable) and pick $p\notin S$.

Since $\varphi$ is satisfiable, there is a valuation $v$ with $v\models\varphi$. The truth value of $\varphi$ under any valuation depends only on the restriction of that valuation to $S$ (because no variable outside $S$ appears in $\varphi$). Define two valuations:

- $v_1$: agrees with $v$ on $S$, and $v_1(p)=1$;
- $v_2$: agrees with $v$ on $S$, and $v_2(p)=0$.

Both $v_1$ and $v_2$ agree with $v$ on $S$, so $v_1\models\varphi$ and $v_2\models\varphi$.

Now consider the two elements $[\varphi\wedge p]$ and $[\varphi\wedge\neg p]$ in $A$:

1. **Both are nonzero.** $v_1\models\varphi\wedge p$, so $\varphi\wedge p$ is satisfiable. $v_2\models\varphi\wedge\neg p$, so $\varphi\wedge\neg p$ is satisfiable.

2. **Both are strictly below $[\varphi]$.** We have $v_2\models\varphi$ but $v_2\not\models\varphi\wedge p$, so $\varphi\wedge p\not\equiv\varphi$, giving $[\varphi\wedge p]<[\varphi]$. Similarly $v_1\models\varphi$ but $v_1\not\models\varphi\wedge\neg p$, so $[\varphi\wedge\neg p]<[\varphi]$.

Therefore $[\varphi]$ is **not** an atom: it has a nonzero element strictly below it.

### Why no formula can be an atom (structural reason)

An atom would correspond to a formula satisfied by a *single* valuation (up to equivalence). Pinning down a single valuation among all $2^{\omega_1}$ valuations requires specifying the truth value of every one of the $\omega_1$ variables—i.e., a conjunction of $\omega_1$ literals. But $L_{\omega_1}$ only permits conjunctions of length $<\omega_1$ (countable), so any formula leaves $\omega_1\setminus S$ (still of cardinality $\omega_1$) variables unspecified, yielding $2^{\omega_1}$ many satisfying valuations. There is always "room" to split.

### Conclusion

Since $[\varphi]$ was an arbitrary nonzero element of $A$ and we exhibited a nonzero element strictly below it, **$A$ has no atoms**.

$$\boxed{A \text{ is atomless; it contains no atoms.}}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
